newsitem.title: CONGO: Fresh shooting but signs of hope in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Fresh shooting but signs of hope in Brazzaville.

text.p: Mediators pursued an elusive deal to end a bloody month-old standoff in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville on Friday despite sporadic shooting around the city centre frontline in the afternoon.

There were signs of hope of a settlement to restore peace to the city where clashes between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and of his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso have killed hundreds of people and put tens of thousands to flight.
Diplomats in Kinshasa, across the Congo River, said Lissouba and Sassou had agreed a truce proposed by international mediator President Omar Bongo of Gabon from midnight (2300 GMT).
"Sassou's people seem to consider the ceasefire as a fait accompli -- provided of course that they don't get fired at," said one diplomat.
Most truces to date have collapsed after a day or so.
Witnesses said there was no apparent focus to Friday's shooting and that some soldiers appeared to be firing for the sake of it.

Hellot Mampouya, spokesman for Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, told Reuters that a national mediation committee led by Kolelas expected to make public the results of its latest negotiations on Saturday.
Kolelas, whose own supporters were at the heart of similar bloody ethnic and political clashes after a disputed 1993 parliamentary election, had talks with both men this week.
Lissouba on Tuesday accepted a nine-point blueprint proposed by Kolelas's committee as a basis for negotiation.
Sassou told national radio on Friday he had replied to Kolelas and his mediation committee in talks on Thursday. He declined to indicate his response but implied he was well disposed to it.

"At the current stage in the negotiations, I have given my answer to the mediation committee," he said, adding: "We are working to lead our people back to peace, to national reconciliation and to well-being."
The showdown began on June 5 when soliders surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militia ahead of a presidential election planned for July 27.
Lissouba, Sassou and Kolelas were all due to run.
One striking change on Friday was a new impartial tone on Radio Congo, the state radio, which in recent weeks has broadcast virulent anti-Sassou propaganda throughout the day.

Radio Congo also highlighted an agreement between France and the United States, often portrayed at loggerheads over foreign policy in Central Africa, "to work hand-in-hand" to try to find a peaceable solution to the Congolese conflict.

In New York, the U.N. Security Council agreed in principle on Thursday to endorse a multinational, mainly African, force for the former French colony but question marks remained over who would pay for the force and who would lead it.
An African peace force in Brazzaville, according to U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, would need voluntary financing and a lead country to organise the operation.
Neither was immediately available, although diplomats said Lissouba's government has offered $1 million for peacekeepers.

Sahnoun told a Thursday news conference later that the 1,000 soldiers should secure Brazzaville airport to make sure new weapons did not arrive and patrol with opposing factions to verify that a ceasefire was honoured.
